entries.title: read_csv(squeeze=True) raises TypeError
entries.body:
`read_csv` no longer accepts the `squeeze` argument. Code that passed `squeeze=True` to get a Series from a one-column file now raises `TypeError`.

Read the file normally and call `.squeeze("columns")` on the result.

The pandas 2.0.0 release notes list `squeeze` among the arguments removed from `read_csv`.
entries.code:
import io
import pandas as pd

csv = "name,score\nAna,10\nBob,12\n"

try:
    pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(csv), index_col=0, squeeze=True)
except TypeError as e:
    print("TypeError:", e)

scores = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(csv), index_col=0).squeeze("columns")
print(scores)
entries.output:
TypeError: read_csv() got an unexpected keyword argument 'squeeze'
name
Ana    10
Bob    12
Name: score, dtype: int64

entries.title: fillna(method=...) raises TypeError
entries.body:
`fillna` no longer takes a `method` argument in the version used for this page. Passing `method="ffill"` raises `TypeError`.

Use `ffill()` to carry the last valid value forward, and `bfill()` to carry the next valid value backward.
entries.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([1.0, None, 3.0])

try:
    s.fillna(method="ffill")
except TypeError as e:
    print("TypeError:", e)

print(s.ffill())
entries.output:
TypeError: NDFrame.fillna() got an unexpected keyword argument 'method'
0    1.0
1    1.0
2    3.0
dtype: float64

entries.title: fillna(inplace=True) on a selected column changes nothing
entries.body:
`df["a"].fillna(0, inplace=True)` fills a temporary object, not the DataFrame. In pandas 3 the DataFrame stays unchanged and pandas emits a `ChainedAssignmentError` warning.

Assign the result back to the column instead: `df["a"] = df["a"].fillna(0)`.

The pandas 3.0.0 release notes describe the Copy-on-Write change behind this behaviour.
entries.code:
import warnings
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1.0, None, 3.0]})

with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    df["a"].fillna(0, inplace=True)
print("warning:", caught[0].category.__name__)
print(df["a"].isna().sum(), "missing value(s) left")

df["a"] = df["a"].fillna(0)
print(df["a"].isna().sum(), "missing value(s) left after assigning back")
entries.output:
warning: ChainedAssignmentError
1 missing value(s) left
0 missing value(s) left after assigning back

entries.title: Chained assignment with a boolean mask no longer updates the DataFrame
entries.body:
`df["a"][df["b"] > 15] = 0` selects a column and then assigns into the result. In pandas 3 the original DataFrame is not modified, and pandas warns with `ChainedAssignmentError`.

Use a single `.loc[row_condition, "column"]` call. It reads like the SQL `UPDATE ... SET a = 0 WHERE b > 15`.

The pandas 3.0.0 release notes cover chained assignment under Copy-on-Write.
entries.code:
import warnings
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3], "b": [10, 20, 30]})

with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    df["a"][df["b"] > 15] = 0
print("warning:", caught[0].category.__name__)
print(df)

df.loc[df["b"] > 15, "a"] = 0
print(df)
entries.output:
warning: ChainedAssignmentError
   a   b
0  1  10
1  2  20
2  3  30
   a   b
0  1  10
1  0  20
2  0  30

entries.title: Setting text into a numeric column raises TypeError
entries.body:
A column has one dtype. Assigning a string into an `int64` column raises `TypeError` instead of converting the whole column to text.

Decide how a missing or unknown value is stored. A float column with `NaN` keeps the numbers usable in calculations. Free-text labels belong in a separate column.
entries.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"n": [1, 2, 3]})

try:
    df.loc[1, "n"] = "unknown"
except TypeError as e:
    print("TypeError:", e)

df["n"] = df["n"].astype("float64")
df.loc[1, "n"] = np.nan
print(df)
entries.output:
TypeError: Invalid value 'unknown' for dtype 'int64'
     n
0  1.0
1  NaN
2  3.0

entries.title: String columns are no longer dtype object
entries.body:
In pandas 3, text columns get the `str` dtype by default instead of `object`. A test such as `df["city"].dtype == object` now returns `False`, so a check written for `object` silently skips those columns.

`select_dtypes(include="object")` still returns them for backward compatibility, but pandas 3.1.0 warns (`Pandas4Warning`) that this will be removed. Select with `include="str"` and test with `pd.api.types.is_string_dtype()`.

The pandas 3.0.0 release notes describe the new default string dtype.
entries.code:
import warnings
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Cluj", "Iasi"], "n": [1, 2]})

print(df["city"].dtype)
print(df["city"].dtype == object)
print(pd.api.types.is_string_dtype(df["city"]))

with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    print(list(df.select_dtypes(include="object").columns))
print("warning:", caught[0].category.__name__)

print(list(df.select_dtypes(include="str").columns))

entries.title: concat with keys and ignore_index=True raises ValueError
entries.body:
`keys` labels each piece in the result index, and `ignore_index=True` throws the index away, so the two cannot be combined. pandas 3 raises `ValueError`.

Pick one. To keep the origin of each row as a column, concatenate with `keys`, then move that index level into a column with `reset_index`.

The pandas 3.0.0 release notes list this change.
entries.code:
import pandas as pd

a = pd.DataFrame({"x": [1]})
b = pd.DataFrame({"x": [2]})

try:
    pd.concat([a, b], keys=["a", "b"], ignore_index=True)
except ValueError as e:
    print("ValueError:", e)

out = pd.concat([a, b], keys=["a", "b"]).reset_index(level=0, names="source").reset_index(drop=True)
print(out)
entries.output:
ValueError: Cannot set ignore_index=True and specify keys. Either should be used.
  source  x
0      a  1
1      b  2

entries.title: merge has no ignore_index argument
entries.body:
`ignore_index` belongs to functions such as `concat`. `DataFrame.merge` does not accept it and raises `TypeError`.

When rows are joined on columns, the result already has a fresh index numbered from 0. Call `reset_index(drop=True)` only if the join was done on the index.
entries.code:
import pandas as pd

left = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2], "v": ["x", "y"]})
right = pd.DataFrame({"id": [2, 1], "w": [20, 10]})

try:
    left.merge(right, on="id", ignore_index=True)
except TypeError as e:
    print("TypeError:", e)

print(left.merge(right, on="id"))
entries.output:
TypeError: DataFrame.merge() got an unexpected keyword argument 'ignore_index'
   id  v   w
0   1  x  10
1   2  y  20

entries.title: Datetimes cast to integers are 1000 times smaller in pandas 3
entries.body:
Parsed date strings now default to microsecond resolution (`datetime64[us]`) instead of nanosecond. Casting to an integer therefore returns microseconds since 1970-01-01, 1000 times smaller than the nanosecond value older code expects. Nothing raises an error, so the wrong numbers can pass unnoticed.

Convert explicitly with `as_unit("ns")` before casting, or avoid integer casts.

The pandas 3.0.0 release notes describe the new resolution inference.
entries.code:
import pandas as pd

dt = pd.to_datetime(["2024-03-22 11:36"])

print(dt.dtype)
print(dt.astype("int64")[0])
print(dt.as_unit("ns").astype("int64")[0])

entries.title: seaborn: x and y must be passed by keyword
entries.body:
Since seaborn 0.12, `data` is the only positional argument of most plotting functions. `sns.scatterplot("x", "y", data=df)` raises `TypeError`.

Pass `data=`, `x=` and `y=` by name.

The seaborn 0.12.0 release notes describe this under keyword-only arguments.
entries.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns

df = pd.DataFrame({"x": [1, 2, 3], "y": [3, 1, 2]})

try:
    sns.scatterplot("x", "y", data=df)
except TypeError as e:
    print("TypeError:", e)

ax = sns.scatterplot(data=df, x="x", y="y")
print(type(ax).__name__)
entries.output:
TypeError: scatterplot() got multiple values for argument 'data'
Axes
